title: Fund fees: the hidden cost you're paying
subtitle: Expense ratio
openingQuestion: Two ETFs both track VN30, with identical index performance. Fund A charges a 0.65%/year management fee, Fund B charges 1.5%/year. After 20 years investing VND 100 million, what happens?
openingOptions: There's no meaningful difference between the two funds, since a management-fee gap of about 0.85%/year is too small a number to worry about
Fund B will definitely deliver a higher return, since a higher management fee always means better service quality
The annual management fee has no effect whatsoever on the final profit the investor receives
Fund A gives a higher final balance, because the lower fee compounds over 20 years
explanation: A fund fee is deducted directly from assets each year so it never appears as an expense you pay - which is exactly why it's easy to underestimate. The problem is that the deducted portion also loses its ability to earn a return in every remaining year, so the gap compounds exponentially rather than adding up linearly. Besides the annual management fee, you should also read the purchase, redemption and switching fees - these are rarely mentioned in marketing material.

realWorldExample.company: Comparing management fees of Vietnam's domestic ETFs
realWorldExample.description: Domestic ETFs tracking VN30 in Vietnam usually have an expense ratio of around 0.6%-1%/year, while some active open-ended funds may charge a 1.5%-2%/year management fee plus issuance/redemption fees. Investors rarely notice this fee because it's quietly deducted from the net asset value (NAV) every day, not shown as a clear deduction on a statement.

quiz.question: What is a fund's expense ratio?
options: A one-time fee paid when buying the fund certificate
The share of fund assets deducted each year for operating costs
A fee paid to the broker each time you place an order
The personal income tax the State collects on fund profit
quiz.explanation: The expense ratio is a fund's annual operating cost (salaries for the management team, trading costs, administrative expenses...), expressed as a percentage of total fund assets, and deducted gradually each day from NAV - meaning investors often don't notice it immediately but are still paying this fee.

quiz.question: Why does a small management-fee gap (like 0.5%/year) have such a large impact long-term?
options: Because the fee is fully refunded after exactly 10 years of holding the fund
Because the fee rate automatically doubles every year of holding
Because the fee deducted each year reduces the capital that compounds
Because a small fee gap actually has no meaningful impact
quiz.explanation: Compounding works both ways - it grows your money, but it also 'compounds' the fee deducted each year because that portion would otherwise have kept earning returns had it not been deducted. The longer the investment horizon, the more that small fee gap magnifies over time.

quiz.question: You invest VND 100 million in a fund with a 1.5%/year expense ratio. That year the fund earns 10%. How much do you actually net?
options: 10 million, since the management fee is paid by the management company itself
1.5 million, since the remaining portion is retained to reinvest for next year throughout every single day of the year
10 million minus personal income tax, the fee doesn't affect anything
8.5 million - the fee is gradually deducted from fund assets throughout the year
quiz.explanation: The fee doesn't appear as a deduction on your statement - it's gradually deducted from the fund's net asset value each day. You only see the final result already net of the fee, which makes this cost very easy to overlook.

quiz.question: Besides the expense ratio, what other fee do fund investors in Vietnam commonly encounter?
options: Purchase and redemption fees on the fund certificate, usually higher if sold early
A mandatory insurance fee on the entire portfolio value each year
A listing fee paid to the exchange, based on number of orders placed, usually disclosed only in the fine print
An audit fee that each investor must pay separately at year-end
quiz.explanation: Many open-ended funds charge a purchase fee (around 0-1%) and a redemption fee that scales with holding period - selling within the first 6 months can cost 1-2%, while holding over 2 years usually drops to zero. This structure encourages long-term holding, but also means redeeming early is expensive.

quiz.question: Why does a fee gap of 1%/year matter far more than it seems?
options: Because the fee doubles every year under how funds currently compute compounding
Because the deducted amount stops earning compound returns later
Because a 1% fee is computed on total profit rather than on the original capital
Because the tax authority levies extra tax on the fee the fund has collected from you
quiz.explanation: Losing 1% this year isn't just losing 1%: that money would otherwise have kept earning returns in every remaining year. With VND 100 million, 20 years and a 10% return, a fee gap of 1%/year makes the final balance differ by about VND 100 million - equal to the entire original capital.

quiz.question: Is the lowest-fee fund always the best choice?
options: Yes, fee is the only factor an investor can control so pick the lowest
Yes, because every fund tracking the same index produces exactly identical results
No - you must also check how closely the fund tracks the index and whether its scale is large enough
No, because low-fee funds usually restrict how many times you're allowed to trade per year which is exactly the point often missed
quiz.explanation: Fee is the most important factor and also the only one you know for certain in advance, but it's not the only one. A cheap fund with a large tracking error or too small a scale (easily closed, poor liquidity) can be worse than a slightly pricier but well-run fund.

keyTakeaways: The expense ratio is a fund's operating fee, quietly but genuinely deducted from assets each year, even though the investor doesn't see a direct deduction
Even a small fee gap (0.5-1%/year) can create a large difference in final balance over decades due to the effect of compounding
Always check the expense ratio before choosing an investment fund, especially for a long-term investment plan

practicePrompt.question: You invest VND 100 million in one of two ETFs both tracking VN30 for 20 years, with an average market return of 10%/year before fees. Fund A charges 0.65%/year, Fund B charges 1.5%/year. Is this 0.85%/year fee difference worth considering?
options: Yes - the fee deducted every year reduces compounding capital, and that gap accumulates over 20 years
No, because a fee gap of only 0.85%/year is too small to create any meaningful difference after 20 years of investing
No, because a fund charging a higher fee always comes with better management service, sufficiently offsetting that fee gap
Yes, but only because Fund B is certain to perform worse at tracking the VN30 index correctly
practicePrompt.explanation: The small annual fee gap is repeatedly deducted from the capital that compounds - over 20 years, that lost compounding accumulates into a significant sum, even though both funds track the same index.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Calculate the impact of fees
application.message: Take a hypothetical VND 100 million investment, and calculate the balance difference yourself after 20 years between a 0.3%/year fee and a 1.5%/year fee at the same gross return.
application.secondary: A concrete number after 20 years is usually more surprising than you'd expect.

sections.text: There's a type of cost very few beginning investors notice, because it never shows up as a clear deduction on a bank statement - that's the fund management fee, also known as the expense ratio.

When you invest in a fund (ETF, open-ended fund, active fund...), that fund needs money to operate: paying the management team's salary, trading costs, custody costs, audit costs, marketing... All of these costs are bundled into a percentage of total fund assets each year, called the expense ratio, and deducted gradually each day from the fund's net asset value (NAV).

Unlike a trading fee (which you see immediately when placing an order), the expense ratio is quietly deducted from NAV every day. For example, a fund with a 1%/year expense ratio has, in effect, a tiny portion (about 1%/365) deducted from asset value each day before you ever see your investment's value. This leaves many people completely unaware they're paying a fee, even though it's steadily eating into returns every day.

items: Expense ratio = Total fund operating cost in the year / Total fund assets
Passive ETFs (tracking an index) usually have a low expense ratio: around 0.3%-1%/year
Active funds usually have a higher expense ratio: 1.5%-2.5%/year or more, due to needing to pay for an analyst team
Some funds also charge a purchase fee (front-end load) or a redemption fee for exiting early (back-end load, issuance/redemption fee)

sections.label: An example with real numbers
sections.text: You invest VND 100 million, assuming an average market return of 10%/year before fees. Fund A charges 0.65%/year, Fund B charges 1.5%/year, with identical pre-fee performance. After 20 years: Fund A might reach around VND 580 million, Fund B only about VND 480 million - a gap of nearly VND 100 million just from a 0.85%/year fee difference, accumulated through the effect of compounding over 20 years.
A low fee doesn't automatically mean a better fund

Worth noting: a low fee is a big plus, but not the only factor for choosing a fund. An active fund with a high fee that genuinely delivers sustainable outperformance over many years (after fees) can still be a good choice. The point is you need to look at post-fee performance (net return) when comparing funds, not just compare fees alone.

lines: The expense ratio is a quiet but very real fee, deducted gradually each day from your asset value.
For long-term investing, even a small fee gap can create a difference of tens of percent in final balance thanks to the effect of compounding.
